power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Humans often learn from outcomes defined by abstract goals rather than explicit rewards.
This flexibility supports real-world behavior but typically causes slower and less efficient learning compared to directly observable rewards.
We asked where the cognitive bottleneck arises as abstract goals are transformed into learning signals.

The reward function compression hypothesis proposes that this inefficiency arises because evaluating abstract goal outcomes burdens limited cognitive resources otherwise directed toward learning, and that this cognitive cost can decrease over iterations when a specialized, efficient goal-dependent outcome evaluation function is learned.
Alternatively, this cost could simply arise from an immediate dual-task effect, where goal maintenance imposes a cost on decisions.
To distinguish these two hypotheses, we manipulated the visibility of goal and non-goal information throughout learning and feedback.

While the memory-offloading account predicts that this manipulation should immediately rescue goal-based learning, the reward function compression hypothesis predicts a gradually acquired benefit proportional to the compressibility of the match/mismatch rule.
Our results (N = 61) supported the reward compression hypothesis.
Visible goals gradually reduced learning efficiency costs, eventually approaching the point-based learning performance.
An equivalent decrease in memory load (visible non-goals) did not boost learning as much, highlighting the role of outcome evaluation in goal-directed learning.

Computational modeling revealed that outcome evaluation efficiency, proxied by participants' "reward collection" response time, specifically influenced participants' learning processes, rather than decision noise.
These results show that learning from goals depends on our ability to train efficient estimators of outcome values, which is facilitated by keeping goals in sight.

In daily life, much of human learning is guided by abstract goals we pursue -such as mastering Chinese calligraphy, finding a favorite hiking route or perfecting a baking recipe -that go beyond obtaining tangible rewards like food or money.
Goals define what we want to achieve and give value to the outcomes of our actions, providing signals that guide learning.
For example, when learning a master calligrapher's style, we compare our brushstrokes with their work to evaluate each attempt and track our progress.
The criteria for this evaluation can change with our subjective goals or the context [Molinaro and Collins, 2023a , Castegnetti et al., 2021 , Frömer et al., 2019].
text.formatted: The criteria for this evaluation can change with our subjective goals or the context <ref type="bibr">[Molinaro and Collins, 2023a</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">, Castegnetti et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">, Frömer et al., 2019]</ref>.

text.text: We may focus on the shape of individual strokes when reproducing a particular model, but place greater weight on the overall flow when aiming for a more expressive style.

Learning guided by goals is therefore highly flexible, but this flexibility requires learners to continually translate outcomes into reinforcement signals that can guide learning, based on their current goals.
The flexibility of goal-dependent learning comes at cognitive cost.

When the value of an outcome must be derived from an abstract goal rather than provided directly by familiar rewards, such as numeric points, learning is slower and SIGHT -NOVEMBER 12, 2026 less accurate [McDougle et al., 2022, Molinaro and Collins, 2023b].
text.formatted: When the value of an outcome must be derived from an abstract goal rather than provided directly by familiar rewards, such as numeric points, learning is slower and <ref type="bibr">SIGHT -NOVEMBER 12, 2026</ref> less accurate <ref type="bibr">[McDougle et al., 2022, Molinaro and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Collins, 2023b]</ref>.

text.text: Despite these behavioral costs, goal-derived and explicit rewards appear to rely on overlapping reward-learning circuitry.

Goal-congruent outcomes evoke reward-like signals in corticostriatal circuits, including shared value representations and reward-prediction-error signals [McDougle et al., 2022]; similarly, cognitive feedback (e.g., a green circle for correct and a red circle for incorrect) and monetary rewards recruit largely overlapping dopaminergic and striatal regions during learning [Daniel and Pollmann, 2010].

text.text: The critical difference may therefore lie not in the downstream learning system itself, but in the additional executive processes required to derive the value of an outcome from the current goal.
Indeed, learning from novel goal-defined outcomes is associated with increased interactions between prefrontal control regions and subcortical reward circuits [McDougle et al., 2022].
text.formatted: Indeed, learning from novel goal-defined outcomes is associated with increased interactions between prefrontal control regions and subcortical reward circuits <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[McDougle et al., 2022]</ref>.

text.text: This raises a central question: which cognitive operations make the transformation from a goal and an observed outcome into a learning signal costly?
Identifying these operations is essential for understanding the cognitive bottleneck of goal-dependent learning.
One possibile cause of this additional cost is the working-memory demand of maintaining the current goal.
In typical goal-dependent learning tasks, learners must actively maintain the goal information until feedback is received [McDougle et al., 2022].
text.formatted: In typical goal-dependent learning tasks, learners must actively maintain the goal information until feedback is received <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[McDougle et al., 2022]</ref>.

text.text: Maintaining goal-relevant information is itself a core function of working memory and cognitive control [Kane and Engle, 2003, Braver, 2012].
text.formatted: Maintaining goal-relevant information is itself a core function of working memory and cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[Kane and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Engle, 2003, Braver, 2012]</ref>.

text.text: Working-memory contributions to learning are capacity limited, with learning performance declining as memory load increases [Collins and Frank, 2012], and imposing an additional working-memory load concurrently with instrumental learning can further impair learning performance [Huang et al., 2025].
text.formatted: Working-memory contributions to learning are capacity limited, with learning performance declining as memory load increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[Collins and Frank, 2012]</ref>, and imposing an additional working-memory load concurrently with instrumental learning can further impair learning performance <ref type="bibr">[Huang et al., 2025]</ref>.

text.text: Maintaining the current goal may therefore consume limited working-memory resources, imposing a relatively general cognitive cost throughout the learning process (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: Maintaining the current goal may therefore consume limited working-memory resources, imposing a relatively general cognitive cost throughout the learning process (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>).

text.text: A second possibility is that the additional cost arises more specifically during outcome evaluation.

Whereas explicit numeric rewards such as (+1) or (+0) directly specify the value of an outcome, abstract feedback must be evaluated relative to the learner's current goal before it can provide a learning signal.
This computation can be described by a reward function evaluation, which assigns value to an outcome according to the current goal.
Recent behavioral work suggests that this goal-dependent outcome evaluation may itself constitute an important bottleneck.

Faster goaldependent reward processing was associated with better learning, and learning improved when the goal space contained structure that allowed goal information to be simplified [Molinaro and Collins, 2026].
text.formatted: Faster goaldependent reward processing was associated with better learning, and learning improved when the goal space contained structure that allowed goal information to be simplified <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[Molinaro and Collins, 2026]</ref>.

text.text: This work proposes that, when the goal space contains shared structure, learners can reduce this cost through reward-function compression, extracting regularities across goals and transforming complex goal information into a simpler rule that can be applied more efficiently when evaluating subsequent outcomes.
Under this account, the additional cognitive demand is concentrated around feedback, when an observed outcome must be converted into a value that can update learning (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: Under this account, the additional cognitive demand is concentrated around feedback, when an observed outcome must be converted into a value that can update learning (Figure <ref type="figure">1B</ref>).

text.text: To distinguish these possible mechanisms, one strategy is to externalize goal information by keeping it visible throughout learning, including when feedback is received.

Externalizing goal-relevant information is common in everyday learning, such as reminders, checklists, and reference materials, which can reduce the need to maintain information internally [Risko and Gilbert, 2016 , Stein et al., 2016 , Gilbert et al., 2020].
text.formatted: Externalizing goal-relevant information is common in everyday learning, such as reminders, checklists, and reference materials, which can reduce the need to maintain information internally <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[Risko and Gilbert, 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">, Stein et al., 2016</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">, Gilbert et al., 2020]</ref>.

text.text: By shifting part of the representational burden from internal memory to the environment, these external cues can preserve access to goal information while freeing limited working-memory resources for other computations involved in learning.
Goal visibility, however, may do more than simply reduce memory load: it may also change how feedback is processed.
If the primary cost arises from goal maintenance, keeping the goal visible should reduce the general working-memory demand of maintaining and retrieving it throughout learning.

If the cost instead arises during outcome evaluation, having the goal visible may allow learners to directly compare an observed outcome with the desired outcome, rather than first retrieving the goal from memory.
Returning to Chinese calligraphy, during línmó practice, learners can keep a master calligrapher's copybook visible while practicing and directly compare each produced stroke with the desired form.
Repeated access to such a reference may also allow learners to develop a simpler, reusable comparison-to-value rule for evaluating subsequent outcomes.

This possibility connects goal visibility to reward-function compression: whereas compression may emerge by extracting structure from internally represented goals, externally available goal information may provide another source of structure that simplifies the computation of outcome value.
A visible non-goal provides an important comparison.
Like a visible goal, it externalizes task-relevant outcome information and may therefore provide similar memory support.

Critically, however, it changes how the external reference must be mapped onto value: a match with a visible goal signals a desirable outcome, whereas a match with a visible non-goal signals an undesirable outcome.

Previous reinforcement-learning studies suggest that positive and negative outcomes can sometimes be weighted differently during learning, although such asymmetries are not universal and may partly reflect other choice processes [Palminteri et al., 2017 , Katahira, 2018 , Sugawara and Katahira, 2021 , Lefebvre et al., 2017 , Frank et al., 2007].

text.text: More broadly, valuation can flexibly reverse with the learner's current goal, such that the same option is processed differently when the goal is to identify the best versus the worst outcome [Frömer et al., 2019].

text.text: Comparing visible goal and visible non-goal conditions can therefore help distinguish a general benefit of externalizing information from a more specific benefit of making the desired outcome directly available during outcome evaluation.
The current study asks how abstract goals are transformed into learning signals and which cognitive operations create the cost of this transformation.
We use goal visibility to probe this process, asking how making goal information externally available facilitates goal-dependent learning and which cognitive operation best explains this benefit.
Specifically, we characterize the visibility benefit along two dimensions: its dynamics over experience and its magnitude across visibility conditions (Figure 1C).
text.formatted: Specifically, we characterize the visibility benefit along two dimensions: its dynamics over experience and its magnitude across visibility conditions (Figure <ref type="figure">1C</ref>).

text.text: First, the time course of the benefit can distinguish a general goal-memory offloading account from an experiencedependent change in outcome evaluation.

If visibility primarily reduces the need to maintain goal information in working memory (Figure 1A), its benefit should be available as soon as the goal is externally accessible, producing an immediate advantage that is already present in Phase 1 and remains in Phase 2 (Figure 1D&E).

text.text: In contrast, if visibility facilitates the development of a more efficient comparison-to-value rule during outcome evaluation (Figure 1B), the benefit may emerge gradually with experience and become larger in Phase 2 (Figure 1F&G).

text.text: Second, the relative magnitude of the VG and VNG benefits can reveal whether the mechanism supported by visibility operates similarly across different external references.

A symmetric benefit would suggest that VG and VNG provide comparable support, either by offloading similar memory demands or by enabling similarly efficient mappings from feedback to value (Figure 1D&F).

text.text: To test whether learning policy parameters varied across block conditions (Points, Goals, VG, and VNG), we fit a family of models in which selected parameters were allowed to vary as a function of block-level characteristics.
Specifically, modulation parameters ω ∈ [-10, 10] scaled the baseline parameter values as a function of the median log reward-collection response time (RCRT) for the corresponding block.
This approach allows us to test whether a parameter changes in different blocks in a way that is systematically captured by differences in reward collection efficiency.
We also compared this to models that used stimulus-action choice reaction times instead of RCRT to ensure the specificity of the findings to outcome evaluation (see S2.3 in Supplementary Materials).

text.text: Model fitting.

Models were fitted separately to each participant by minimizing the negative log-likelihood using the L-BFGS-B optimization algorithm implemented in scipy.optimize.minimize with bound constraints on all free parameters and multiple initializations.
The optimization was repeated from 40 starting points, including one default initialization and multiple random initializations, and the best-fitting solution was retained.
Model comparison.
Models were compared using the Akaike information criterion (AIC): where k is the number of free parameters.
Model evidence was summarized using participant-level ∆AIC, group mean ∆AIC with standard errors, and the proportion of participants best fitted by each model.
Subject-level ∆AIC values were tested against zero using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
Model comparison proceeded in stages.

First, simpler models with fixed parameter values ablating specific mechanisms (e.g. decay, learning asymmetry, mixture) were compared with the full model to assess the contribution of individual model components.
Second, static-and dynamic-noise models were compared.
Third, we compared models in which RCRT separately modulated each parameter to identify which parameter yielded the greatest improvement in model fit.
Fourth, we compared RCRT with choice RT, hit RCRT, and correct-rejection RCRT to test whether block RCRT provided a better account of choice behavior than the alternative reaction-time measures.
To validate the winning model against competing models, 40 agents were simulated for each participant and model using the participant-specific fitted parameters and observed task structure.
Behavioral measures were first averaged across simulated agents within each participant and then summarized across participants.
Model validation assessed how well each model reproduced the observed learning curves and participant-level accuracy.
We sought to verify model identifiability within groups of models we relied on to arbitrate between competing accounts of our findings.

Specifically, we separately assessed identifiability of the best three single-parameter modulation models (α, κ, and ϕ); and identifiability of the full three-parameter modulation model, the p ER -modulated, and a baseline model.
For each participant and generating model, we simulated 10 datasets using participant-specific fitted parameters.
We refitted all three models in the corresponding comparison set to each dataset and identified the recovered model by the lowest AIC among converged fits.
Results were summarized in row-normalized confusion matrices.

In this study, we investigated which cognitive processes contribute to the cost of transforming abstract goals into learning signals by manipulating the visibility of goal information during learning and feedback.
Consistent with prior work, learning from goal-dependent outcomes impose a learning cost relative to explicit point feedback [McDougle et al., 2022, Molinaro and Collins, 2026].
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work, learning from goal-dependent outcomes impose a learning cost relative to explicit point feedback <ref type="bibr">[McDougle et al., 2022, Molinaro and</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Collins, 2026]</ref>.

text.text: Making goal information externally available substantially reduced this cost, but critically, the benefit of visibility was not static: performance in the visible conditions (VG and VNG) improved across learning phases, with the largest gain in VG, which ultimately converged to the numeric point-based performance.

This temporal pattern is difficult to explain by a purely static memory-offloading account, under which the benefit of externalizing goal information should be available as soon as that information becomes visible.
Instead, the gradual increase in the visibility benefit is more consistent with an experience-dependent change in outcome evaluation.

In line with the reward-function compression account [Molinaro and Collins, 2026], repeated access to external goal information may support the development of a simpler and more efficient mapping from observed outcomes to value.
text.formatted: In line with the reward-function compression account <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[Molinaro and Collins, 2026]</ref>, repeated access to external goal information may support the development of a simpler and more efficient mapping from observed outcomes to value.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that the central cognitive bottleneck in goal-dependent learning arises from outcome evaluation, when goal information must be used to transform observed feedback into a value that can guide learning.
Our findings build on prior work [McDougle et al., 2022 , Molinaro and Collins, 2023b , 2026] to extend the idea of reward function compression to a new setting.

text.text: In earlier work, reward function compression was primarily described as arising from the structure of the goal space itself: simpler goal spaces, and more commonalities across concurrently pursued goals allow for faster learning of an efficient outcome evaluation function [Molinaro and Collins, 2026].
text.formatted: In earlier work, reward function compression was primarily described as arising from the structure of the goal space itself: simpler goal spaces, and more commonalities across concurrently pursued goals allow for faster learning of an efficient outcome evaluation function <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[Molinaro and Collins, 2026]</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, the underlying goal space remained large and unstructured across conditions; instead, visibility provided a stable external reference for evaluating the outcome from a single match or non match feature.
With experience, repeated access to this reference may allow learners to develop a simpler and more reusable mapping from outcome comparison to value.

Our findings therefore suggest that efficient reward-function learning may flexibly exploit structure that enables a more direct mapping from outcomes to value, including structure provided externally through goal visibility at the time of outcome evaluation.
This possibility raises important questions about the scope and generalizability of learned reward functions, as well as how such efficient reward functions are constructed in the first place.
The asymmetric benefit of goal visibility provides further insight into how external information supports outcome evaluation.

Although VG and VNG were designed to provide comparable external memory support, VG showed a substantially larger improvement, suggesting that outcome evaluation remained more costly in VNG even when the relevant information was externally available.
At least two explanations could account for these additional demands.
One possibility is that the two conditions differ in the computation required to map perceptual comparison onto value.

In VG, a match between feedback and the visible reference directly signals a desirable outcome, whereas in VNG, a match signals an undesirable outcome and value must instead be inferred from a mismatch.
Match-and mismatch-based comparisons can differ in processing demands [Farell, 1985 , Egeth, 1966], potentially making the VNG mapping less efficient.
text.formatted: Match-and mismatch-based comparisons can differ in processing demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[Farell, 1985</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">, Egeth, 1966]</ref>, potentially making the VNG mapping less efficient.

text.text: A second possibility is that VNG may be disadvantaged by a more general Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT)-like process.
Because the visible non-goal represents an outcome that should be avoided, the cue itself may acquire negative or avoidance-related valence.

This cue-driven response could compete with the task-defined evaluation of the feedback, biasing outcome processing away from the value specified by the current goal and toward the valence carried by the visible cue itself [Huys et al., 2011].
text.formatted: This cue-driven response could compete with the task-defined evaluation of the feedback, biasing outcome processing away from the value specified by the current goal and toward the valence carried by the visible cue itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[Huys et al., 2011]</ref>.

text.text: Under this account, the additional cost in VNG arises from resolving a conflict between an automatically evoked avoidance tendency and the instrumental value that should guide learning.

Our follow-up analyses suggest these accounts may be intertwined, with their relative influence shifting across the course of learning: in early learning, a general PIT-like approach-avoidance bias may have limited VNG performance, as VNG showed no immedate match-based advantage and was less accurate than VG; later in learning, match-/mismatch-based reward evaluation may have become more influential, as VNG reached comparable accuracy and showed clearer performance gains, potentially offsetting the earlier PIT-like disadvantage (Figure S8 in the Supplementary Materials).

text.text: The behavioral and computational relationship between reward-collection response time (RCRT) and learning provides converging evidence that the efficiency of outcome evaluation shapes subsequent learning.
Behaviorally, RCRT, used here as a readout of outcome-valuation efficiency, tracked individual differences in learning performance.

Computationally, RCRT was associated with multiple learning-and decision-related mechanisms, including learning rate, forgetting, and the balance between value-based and habitual policies, suggesting that its influence was not restricted to a single component of learning.
Specifically, faster RCRT was associated with more effective value updating, consistent with prior work linking reward-processing efficiency to learning rate [Molinaro and Collins, 2026].

text.text: Slower RCRT predicted faster decay of learned values, suggesting that inefficient outcome evaluation made value representations more vulnerable to forgetting or interference from previous trials [Collins, 2025 , Collins et al., 2017 , Collins and Frank, 2012].

text.text: As learned values become less stable, behavior may consequently rely less on value-based control and relatively more on habitual or repetition-based policies [Collins, 2025].

text.text: Several additional analyses suggest that these relationships were specific to outcome evaluation rather than reflecting general differences in response speed or task engagement.
The qualitative pattern of RCRT modulation was consistent across dynamic-and static-noise models, indicating that the effects were robust to how engagement dynamics were modeled.
Moreover, the effects were specific to RCRT, driven primarily by hit-trial RCRT (Figure ??

RCRT also showed little association with parameters related to non-learning or non-policy processes such as choice noise, choice stickiness, and the habit process itself.

Together, these converging results suggest that RCRT reflects variation in outcome-evaluation efficiency that is specifically linked to how stimulus-action values are acquired, maintained, and expressed in choice, rather than general motor speed, response variability, or task engagement.
The retention results further suggest that working-memory resources may have been allocated differently across learning conditions.
Although Points showed the highest accuracy at test, its decline from late learning to testing was greater than that observed in Goal.

One possible explanation is that explicit point feedback required fewer working-memory resources for goal maintenance and outcome evaluation, leaving more capacity available to temporarily support stimulusaction associations during learning .

This temporary support may have boosted learning performance but blocked more sustained learning, as revealed once working memory was no longer available at test [Collins, 2018 , Collins et al., 2017 , Collins and Frank, 2018].

text.text: Goal-dependent learning may instead have recruited more working-memory resources for maintaining goal information and evaluating outcomes, leaving less temporary support for stimulus-action associations.

The model-implied relationship between RCRT and ϕ is compatible with differences in the stability of learned values during learning, but ϕ does not directly measure how working memory was allocated across goal maintenance, outcome evaluation, and stimulus-action learning.
We therefore view this account as a possible explanation of the Points-Goal retention difference, rather than a mechanism established by the present analyses.

More broadly, our findings contribute to a growing view emphasizing that reward is not a fixed property of outcome, but is constructed relative to the learner's current goal during learning and decision making [Juechems and Summerfield, 2019].

text.text: Beyond valuation, goals also organize decision making by prioritizing goal-relevant information and supporting commitment to ongoing objectives [Holton et al., 2024 [Holton et al., , 2025]].

text.text: Goals, thereby, shape the representations that support flexible decisions, such that different features of the same object become relevant depending on their usefulness for the current objective [Castegnetti et al., 2021].

text.text: This flexibility is typically considered in terms of changes in the goal itself: pursuing a different goal changes which features of an outcome are relevant and how that outcome is valued.
Our findings highlight a complementary source of flexibility.
Even when the goal itself remains unchanged, changing how goal information is represented and made available can alter the efficiency with which outcomes are evaluated.
Goal-dependent learning may therefore depend not only on what goal is pursued, but also on how that goal is represented and accessed during learning.
This perspective also connects goal-dependent learning to broader accounts of distributed cognition and external representation.

People routinely use the environment to offload information that would otherwise need to be maintained or manipulated internally, reducing reliance on limited cognitive resources [Intons-Peterson and Fournier, 1986 , Schönpflug, 1986 , Risko and Gilbert, 2016].

text.text: Importantly, however, external representations can do more than support memory: by making task-relevant relations directly available to perception, they can also change the computations required to perform a task [Larkin and Simon, 1987 , Zhang and Norman, 1994 , Kirsh, 2010].

text.text: Keeping goal information visible may similarly reduce the need to maintain it internally, but more importantly, it provides an external reference that can simplify the computation of outcome value.

This principle aligns with work on external representations in education and interface design, which emphasizes that representations are most useful when they make task-relevant relations easier to perceive or compute, rather than simply providing additional information [Ainsworth, 2006, Scaife and Rogers, 1996].

text.text: Our findings suggest a corresponding design principle for goal-dependent learning: an effective goal representation should not only remind learners what they are trying to achieve, but also make it easier to evaluate their current performance relative to that desired state.

Reference examples, progress displays, and other goal representations may therefore be particularly useful when they support a direct comparison between the learner's current outcome and the goal they are trying to reach, much as a visible copybook supports direct comparison during Chinese calligraphy línmó practice.
In sum, our findings suggest that a key cognitive bottleneck in goal-dependent learning lies in outcome evaluation: how efficiently observed outcomes can be translated into value to guide learning.
Making goal information visible facilitated this process and, with experience, substantially improved learning.

The present work extends the reward-function compression account beyond the internal structure of the goal space by raising the possibility that efficient valuation can also be supported by structure available during outcome evaluation.
More broadly, these findings suggest that how goals are represented and made available can be leveraged to facilitate learning.

text.text: To better understand the asymmetry between VG and VNG, we analyzed reward-collection performance and reward collection response time (RCRT) separately for hit (when a goal was obtained) and correct-rejection trials (when a non-goal was obtained).
This analysis was intended to inform the potential explanations of the VG-VNG asymmetry: increased mismatch-based comparison effort or general Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (PIT)-like.
Under the mismatchbased comparison effort account, performance depends on the demands of outcome evaluation itself.

Specifically, the outcome must be compared against the goal representation to determine whether it signals reward, and mismatch-based comparisons are hypothesized to be more effortful and slower than match-based comparisons.

Under the PIT-like account, VNG is expected to be generally disadvantaged because non-goal images carry a less favorable valence, promoting avoidance, but are present on the screen when a goal outcome is obtained, whereas goal outcomes in VG carry a more favorable valence, further promoting approach in correct trials.

Trial-wise accuracy (hits vs. misses; correct rejections vs. false alarms) was analyzed using generalized linear mixedeffects models (GLMMs) with condition, phase, block (included as a control covariate), and the condition × phase interaction as fixed effects, along with a random intercept for subjects.
Trial-wise RCRT was analyzed using Gamma GLMMs with a log link and the same fixed-and random-effects structure.
Pairwise comparisons were Holm-corrected.
Because our theoretical question centered on the asymmetry between the two visible-goal conditions, we focused primarily on the VG-VNG comparison.
We also considered phase-specific effects, because changes across phases were informative for distinguishing between the two accounts.
Accordingly, we report the phase-specific comparisons for Phase 1 and Phase 2 separately, as well as the overall effect across Phase 1&2

text.text: These results showed that the VNG advantage in correct-rejection trials emerged gradually across learning.
Early in learning, VNG did not show a response-time benefit and even showed lower accuracy than VG, but by Phase 2, it achieved similarly high accuracy while showing faster RCRT than VG.
Notably, this Phase 2 effect was strong enough that the across-phase average largely reflected the later-emerging VNG advantage.
Taken together, these results raise the possibility that the PIT-like account and the mismatch-cost account may be intertwined, with their relative influence shifting over the course of learning.
Early in learning, PIT-like effects may be more dominant, as VNG did not immediately show the expected benefit of a match-based comparison.
By Phase 2, however, match-based comparison benefits appeared to become more dominant, as VNG showed clearer performance gains, potentially offsetting the earlier PIT-like disadvantage.
We treat this interpretation as exploratory, and further experiments will be needed to test it directly.
